classification.difficultyReason: Requires three-set inclusion–exclusion and distinguishing pairwise intersections from students studying exactly two languages.

content.prompt: There are seventy Year 11 students at a school and each of them studies at least one of three languages. Thirty students are studying French, forty-five are studying Chinese, thirty are studying German, and five are studying all three languages. How many students are studying exactly two languages?

answer.short:
25 students.

Use three-set inclusion–exclusion, then subtract the three counts of students studying all three languages from the sum of pairwise intersections.
answer.worked:
Let $F$, $C$ and $G$ be the sets of students studying French, Chinese and German. Let $S=|F\cap C|+|F\cap G|+|C\cap G|$. By inclusion–exclusion,
$$\begin{align*}|F\cup C\cup G|&=|F|+|C|+|G|-S+|F\cap C\cap G|\\70&=30+45+30-S+5\\S&=30+45+30+5-70\\S&=40.\end{align*}$$
Each student studying exactly two languages is counted once in $S$, while each student studying all three is counted three times. Hence the number $N$ studying exactly two languages is
$$\begin{align*}N&=S-3|F\cap C\cap G|\\N&=40-3\times5\\N&=25.\end{align*}$$
Therefore, 25 students study exactly two languages.
